chapter_title: Toys and Games (Picture Reading) (Toys and Games)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.activity_title: Picture Walk — Discovering the Outdoor Play Scene

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Look at the picture and answer (pp.37–38): count children, girls, boys, women, and animals.

time_bands.activity: Teacher conducts an unhurried picture walk through the full-page outdoor scene on pp.36–37, pointing to each group in turn — boys crouching with marbles, the girl on the hopscotch grid, the kite flyer — and eliciting one-word observations from the class.
Teacher reads aloud the picture-description text on p.38, pausing at each named activity so children can locate it in the picture.

Look at the picture and answer (pp.37–38): children work individually to count and write the numbers of children, girls, boys, women, and animals in the blanks provided. Teacher circulates to support counting.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this level often count all figures together without sorting by category; encourage them to point to each figure and place it in one group before writing. The picture on pp.36–37 is large and detailed — give the class adequate time to scan each corner before the counting task begins.

periods.activity_title: Picture Comprehension — People, Actions and Playthings

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Look at the picture and answer (pp.37–38): who reads the newspaper, what children play with, and what the old man does.

time_bands.activity: A quick paired chant: teacher reads the six scenes from the picture (marbles, hopscotch, tops, blindfold, kite, reading) and children echo each one, pointing to it in the textbook picture on pp.36–37.

Look at the picture and answer (pp.37–38): teacher poses questions 6, 7, and 8 aloud — who is reading the newspaper, what the children are playing with, and what the old man is doing — children discuss in pairs, then share answers aloud before writing.

Point out activity (p.38): teacher reads each of the five statements aloud (boys with marbles, girl with hopscotch, spinning tops, blindfolded boy, boy with kite) and invites individual children to point to that person in the picture and confirm in a sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: Having scanned and counted the figures in the outdoor play scene, children now read the scene for meaning — focus their attention on what specific individuals are doing rather than how many there are. The old man's role (watching, not playing) is a common source of confusion; guide children to look at his posture and position in the picture rather than guessing.

periods.activity_title: Talking About the Picture — Games, Spaces and People

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Look at the picture and answer (pp.37–38): what games children play, where the class usually plays, and what non-playing children and women are doing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the full-page picture on pp.36–37, pointing to the open space in front of the houses and asking: 'What do you notice about where these children are playing?' Children respond freely in words or phrases.

Guided conversation using questions 2–5 (pp.37–38): teacher leads the class through four prompts — what games the children are playing, where the children in the class usually play, what the non-playing children are doing, and what the women are doing — children take turns answering in full sentences while classmates listen and add.

Teacher invites two or three children to stand and describe one person from the picture in two sentences without naming the activity, while the class listens and guesses who is being described; teacher praises precise vocabulary (crouching, spinning, blindfolded).

periods.teacher_notes: Having identified the games and people through reading activities on the outdoor play scene, children now voice their own experiences — accept answers about any play space (street, yard, school) without correction. Children often list games without constructing a sentence; model the pattern 'The boys are playing…' before inviting responses.

periods.activity_title: Speaking From the Picture — Favourite Games and Imagination

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Look at the picture and answer (pp.37–38): favourite game, and which game in the picture the child would join.

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up the textbook open to the outdoor scene on pp.36–37 and asks: 'If you could step into this picture, which game would call out to you first?' Children think quietly for a moment before the discussion begins.

Describing-experiences round using questions 9–10 (pp.37–38): each child answers in two turns — first naming their favourite game and saying one thing they like about it, then pointing to the game in the picture they would play and explaining why; teacher keeps the pace brisk and prompts with 'because…' where children stop at one word.

Teacher leads a quick class survey: children raise their hands for each game shown in the picture (marbles, hopscotch, tops, kite) as teacher names them, then the class announces which game was the most popular and which was the least.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed the scene from an observer's point of view while talking about games and spaces, children now speak from personal experience — this shift from observation to expression is the key move in this unit. Children who say only a game name should be gently prompted: 'Can you tell us one thing about how you play it?'

periods.activity_title: Naming Playthings — Word Recognition and Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: B — Identify playthings (p.38): write the name of each plaything (marbles, top, skipping rope) below its picture.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the three plaything names — marbles, top, skipping rope — on the board one by one, pointing to each object in the picture on pp.36–37 as she writes; children repeat each word chorally, clapping its syllables.

Word-building activity: teacher erases one letter at a time from each word on the board, asking children to supply the missing letter from memory; pairs help each other re-spell the complete word before it is restored.

B — Identify playthings (p.38): children look at the three small illustrations on p.38, identify each plaything, and write its name in the blank below the picture; teacher moves around to check letter formation and spelling.

Quick consolidation: teacher holds the board and points to one of the three written words; children must point to the matching object in the textbook picture (pp.36–37) and say a sentence using that word — 'The boys are playing with marbles.'

periods.teacher_notes: Having spoken at length about the games shown in the outdoor scene, children now consolidate the vocabulary of playthings through writing — the move from spoken word to written label is the central skill here. 'Skipping rope' is two words and children commonly run them together or omit 'rope'; draw attention to both words during the board work.

periods.activity_title: Bringing It All Together — Picture, Words and Voices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Look at the picture and answer (pp.37–38): identify and describe the activities of different people in the scene.
Look at the picture and answer (pp.37–38): retell the scene using the names of games and people.
B — Identify playthings (p.38): word game using marbles, top, skipping rope.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the textbook to the full-page outdoor scene on pp.36–37 and invites children to look at it silently for a moment, then asks: 'Tell me everything you can see' — accepting contributions about games, people, and objects without correction, building a spoken inventory of the scene.

Retelling round: teacher points to each group in the picture in turn (boys with marbles, girl on hopscotch grid, tops pair, blindfolded boy, kite holder, women on doorstep, old man) and calls on individual children to say one complete sentence about that person — drawing on their understanding of the outdoor play scene.

Word game: teacher describes a plaything from the scene in two clues without naming it ('It is round and small. You roll it on the ground.') and the class calls out the name; children take turns giving their own two-clue descriptions for marbles, top, and skipping rope while classmates guess and then spell the word aloud.

Closing discussion: teacher asks two final questions — 'Which person in this picture would you most like to be, and why?' and 'Which game from this picture could your class play together at school?' — children respond briefly, ending the unit on a personal and imaginative note.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the reading, speaking, and word knowledge built across the outdoor play scene — the retelling round is the central synthesis move, connecting picture observation with spoken sentence construction and vocabulary recall. Where children hesitate during the retelling, point silently to the relevant part of the picture rather than supplying the answer; the picture itself is the scaffold.

items.source_context: Outdoor play scene: children playing marbles, hopscotch, tops, kite; women on doorstep; old man watching.
items.item_stem: Look at the outdoor play scene on Textbook pages 36–37. Which of the following best describes what the old man in the picture is doing?

options.label: B
options.text: He is standing and watching the children play.

options.label: C
options.text: He is playing marbles with the boys.

options.label: D
options.text: He is sitting on the doorstep making a garland.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may have noticed the kite overhead and assumed the old man is the one flying it.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may have grouped the old man with the boys nearest to him in the picture.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may have confused the old man's standing posture with the women seated on the doorstep.

items.item_stem: Look at the outdoor play scene on Textbook pages 36–37. The children in the picture are playing in the open space in front of their homes. Which of the following is the best description of where the children are playing?

options.label: B
options.text: In the open space in front of their houses.

options.label: C
options.text: On a large sports field far from home.

options.label: D
options.text: In a park with benches and fountains.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may be associating organised group play with school rather than a home setting.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may not have noticed the houses and doorstep figures that locate the scene.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may be drawing on experience of public parks rather than reading the picture carefully.
